elements.text: What is the strategy for reducing thrashing? Is the idea just that the whole process is taking up too much RAM?

elements.text:
I'm making the two query changes discussed in the meeting a few weeks ago. The process doesn't take too much RAM. It always uses all available RAM. The confirmation queries, on lower RAM machines, can result in thrashing (quadratic paging) because of the need to read all over certain tables. memory maps can only be read from disk at the granularity of a page, even if just reading one byte.

Controlling paging is the central issue in a memory map store design. This can be done by improving the efficiency of queries, which takes various forms. The query changes I'm implementing consist of (1) using a intermediate table to cache the store identifiers of prevouts spent by inputs, while the inputs are being validated against the prevouts. This precludes the need to perform the prevout lookup twice, in exchange for a modest amount of data. The data can be stored and retrieved in a unitary memory chunk per block, with no search paging. This part is complete and has improved speed, but as expected is not sufficient to prevent thrashing on the mini.

The other (2) change is to consolidate the "point" table into the "spend" table. Point is a lookup table to spent point hashes. This is a tradeoff in query complexity in exchange for reduced storage space (about 50GB saved). This is because point hashes are redundant (multiple outputs per tx, indexed by 32 byte hash in the spending inputs). However the optimization results in thrashing on the mini, and slows sync somewhat on the maxi, so we haven't been using it. Removing it will significantly reduce paging and may therefore eliminate thrashing on the mini.

elements.text: I've completed evaluations of consolidation of the point and spend tables. Turns out this is a bust on both big and small boxes. It takes about 1.5x on the big box, even before becoming memory bound. The extra time is spent in comparisons of search keys. This amounts to memory I/O to perform the comparisons (not even paging because the entire store is memory resident). One of the advantages of splitting the tables was to make search against either of them less costly due to reduced paging and increased locality, despite it taking about 20GiB more space when not utilizing hash consolidation. Turns out that's a significant benefit. On the mini the performance hit is the same up until thrashing kicks in. So I'll stick this work in a dead branch and revert, while cherry picking a couple of small improvements.

elements.text:
I immediately went back to first principles to see if there is some other way to approach it. There are 2 queries that make up the confirmation process (3 if bip30 is active, which it never is). One of the queries is inclusive and the other is exclusive. Inclusive means we check to ensure that the prevouts are confirmed. One confirmation is all we expect/need, and we find it quickly. The other is to ensure that there is no confirmed spender of each external (not in-the-same-block) prevout. This is exclusive - we must exclude all possible spenders. Since we allow conflicting and redundant blocks and txs, and we store them all in the same space, we must ensure that none of them that spend the prevout are presently confirmed (this is during confirmation, so there is no race).

This exhaustive search is to identify any confirmed spend is costly, as the natural point (hash/index), and is the only thing that correlates the spends. Spends are in another table, indexed by the point that they spend - but not the natural point, what I call a "foreign point" which is the primary key of the tx hash (4) in the point table, and the index (3) or 7 bytes. So finding all of the confirmed spenders of a point logically requires reading the spend, transiting to the point table, getting the hash (32) and then searching the point table for all identical hashes, and obtaining the set of point primary keys. Then the index is used to formulate the set of foreign points, and these are used to search the spend hash table. In doing so we exclude the spend that we are presently evaluating. Any other spends are then transitioned to their parent tx primary, which is then searched in the strong_tx table (for confirmedness)...

elements.text:
A recent change I had made to the first query was to expect success (prevout confirmed) and only if it is not confirmed, search for other possible identical transactions (same but with other ids) in the strong_tx table. This is costly, but rare. In a normal run there are only two duplicate txs (bip30 exceptions) and these don't spend. So performing the extra step as necessary is essentially free.

The second query is a different problem, because the search must be exhaustive. The issue then is that txs with the same hash don't have the same primary key, so natural keys (tx hash) must be searched to correlate both spends and confirmations. But we cannot ensure that no duplicates enter the store, as that requires a search for every insert. That tight coupling makes archival (download) very slow. However, the hashmap hash of each identical hashmap element must of course be the same. These duplicates show up as hashmap conflicts and we simply walk the conflict list using an iterator to key on matching search keys, which makes any hash table a multimap.

elements.text: Spend search keys are the primary key of the point table, concatenated to the 3 byte point index. The point pk of course varies even for identical point hashes. It's just the record offset in the point table. However, if we index the spend table not on the primary key of the point, but instead on the search key of the point (point table hash function of the point hash), all spends of the same point would have the same search key, and would therefore be directly identifiable in the spend table iterator. However, conflicts could not be resolved without reading the actual point hash from the point table.

elements.text: Our hashmap functions for sha256-hash keyed hashmaps is a no-op. It's just the low order bytes of the hashes. So not only is it a good distribution, but we can obtain it at no cost. But this isn't the most interesting aspect. By making the spend table search key a function of the point hash, all conflicting spends would necessarily share the same spend table search key. So it is unnecessary to read the point table at all unless there is a conflict. It's not necessary to know the point hash, as the spend for which we are investigating conflicts is already indexed with the foreign point that all conflicting spends must have. This would be the case if the point table was guaranteed to be unique, but it cannot be. So if there are no conflicts with the foreign point of the spend (i.e. a search finds only itself) then there is never a read of the point table during the search. And if there is a conflict in the spend search, the spend can directly identify its point (which it presently does via the foreign point). This implies extra bytes per spend to account for the hash function value in the search key while retaining the point pk.

elements.text: In the above table, there would be over 300k spends that would encounter no conflict (14%). This means that the point table would now be unsearched for each of these - never even accessed. Singular entries in the spend table multimap would imply the current spend is the only spend (which is verified at no cost by comparing the spend pks). The remainder would compare hashes in the point table for each conflict that is not self. That reduces to n-1 hash compare for each n conflicts. So for 2 conflicts above (41% of all spends) that's one sha256 compare in the point table. This drops off logarithmically, 31% require 2 compares, 12% require 3 , and the rest is inconsequential. And again, no searching and comparing all conflicts in the point table. The cost tradeoff is 4 bytes extra per spend. That's not trivial, presently 49GiB (7% increase).

elements.text: Another related consideration is that of strong_tx indexing. Presently the tx table pk is the search key for the strong_tx table. This means that the same tx can be strong (confirmed) under any of the pks under which it may be stored. This means that the exhaustive search above must exhaust them all. This means searching the tx hashmap (using the sha256 hash of the tx) to obtain the pks, until all are excluded. I've considered indexing this table on the hashmap hash of the tx's sha256 hash a well. This would also require secondary conflict resolution, but would preclude searching the tx table or using the 32 byte search key. This resolution could be satisfied by storing the pk of the specific tx confirmed in the row. This would then allow for an immediate search using information immediately available in the spend row (the hashmap hash of the tx sha256 hash is the spend search key), which would eliminate any tx table searching. The implied storage cost is 4 bytes per tx, presently 3.8GiB.

elements.text:
On the maxi I took another look at the performance analyzer during confirmation on the maxi. There are three concurrent loops for each block being confirmed: get-spends, is-spendable, is-spent. I previously spent a bunch of time organizing these in different groups with parallelism and without, and this was the most optimal. But still, the std lib loops are very inefficient. About 75% of all confirmation time on the maxi is spent in lock contention. The locks aren't guarding read/write - they are only providing thread synchronization for the loops.

The database mutexes for hashmap headers, table allocators, and remap safety are all in place as well, but they are inconsequential - because there are very few writes occurring. So is appears that confirmation (absent thrashing) can be significantly optimized during IBD by performing more of the calculations concurrently by block (i.e. as part of validation) and using more storage (as we've done with the prevout table). The only aspect of confirmation that must be sequential by block is checking for spentness (i.e. query against the strong_tx table). So in theory we can produce an ordered list of tx ids to check for spentness by block, followed by writing spentness for each block.tx.

Double spend checks are most expensive, as they require exhaustive search, however they rarely require a check for spentness, because double spends (duplicate tx storage or actual invalidity) are rare. So this is almost no storage and can be made concurrent (*). Confirmedness of prevouts just requires identifying all of the prevout tx pks and storing them until the confirmation stage. IOW, there would be a set of positive and negative tx pks checks for each block, which could just take the place of the data already stored into the prevout table, and would be the same size (4 bytes per spend), and would also be temporary (deletable).

Given that we already use this temporary space and already cover the work distribution cost during validation, and that the concurrent part of confirmation would add no writes, it should be possible to significantly accelerate confirmation as long as the additional reads do not cause thrashing. Despite the fact that we read the entire block and previous outputs for validation, we never search the spend table. That's the big difference in terms of paging, as we must search for all spenders (even though we generally don't find any).

But in the case of thrashing if this is run during validation, it could just be split out to an independent concurrent phase. So I think we can get much more concurrency out of confirmation.

elements.text: Also, we have a third part single file lib included in system now that provides support for std lib concurrent loops for gcc and clang. But it also adds additional performance optimization such as thread pooling (which supports all platforms including msvc). This alone should eliminate most of the lock contention, because it's most likely arising from thread create and release (the std lib doesn't use pools). I think we could get confirmation down to 20 minutes on the maxi (just by eliminating lock contention), for a < 4 hour full validation/confirmation run.

I completed the above test runs on maxi and mini, and there is no consequential change, though the code is simpler. I was also able to remove the search (hashmap) index from the point table, which saved 4 bytes per row plus the header, or 12GiB.

I've concluded that on the mini nothing will get faster as long as the same amount of confirmation paging is required. Based on a lot of inspection I can see that the is-spent exhaustive search over the spend table is where the real cost is. The only way I can see to reduce paging from this is to remove all data not necessary to the search. IOW make it a simple index that points to the remaining data. There is already structure for this, as the spend points to the point table, where the prevout hash is stored. So I can move the parent and input pointers, and the input.sequence value (12 bytes) to the point table. This moves 29GiB (40%) out of the spend table. This will definitely reduce spend query paging, and given that the point hash is already necessary for reading and writing a tx, moving the sequence there isn't an extra cost for download/validate. It does increase the point table, which increases paging there, but we don't do that for spend hashmap conflicts, so should save a lot of paging overall. Relatively simple change as well.

On the maxi I believe that implementing the custom std lib concurrency replacement (required for gcc/clang anyway) with a thread pool may significantly improve performance, because the main limitation there (about 75% cost) is lock contention.

Ok, std lib concurrency support for all compilers is now merged. Performance on the big box looks similar to before (I enabled it always even though msvc does have native support for c++17  concurrency). Now that the locks are identifiably different in the perf monitor I can see that loop synchronization cost is now relatively low, a couple percent. The locking cost in the confirmation query is therefore coming from the hashmap headers and/or table read pointer. With heavy read/write concurrency, as happens on the big box due to heavy archival at the same time as heavy query, lock contention gets pretty significant.

This could be eliminated entirely by isolating the phases and even removing the locks entirely with write suspended during the confirm phase. This could be done with dual table implementations templatized for one to exclude locks altogether. Hard to say for sure if it would be a benefit, since each lock is waiting on actual work on other threads, and this work is absolutely trivial (eg write of one word). The mutexes however do have overhead, and it may be possible to reduce this. But that's getting into the finer details of optimization which are still premature.

I've implemented the change above, making the spend table into a pure index and moving its values to the point table. This required a net increase of 5.3GiB overall, after the removal of the hashmap in the point table, and the net increase of 3 bytes per spend due to redundant storage of the input.point.index in the spend index and the point table. The schema and query changes were pretty significant, affecting a lot of tests. So I'm going to run through it first and see how it looks before burning the time on test updates.

Otherwise the net result is a change in relative size of the two tables. Previously point and spend were 94 and 63 GiB respectively. Now they are 126 and 39GiB. This is the intended reduction of the spend index, as it is used for exhaustive search. This should cut paging by at least 40%. However there are other query simplifications that should reduce paging even further.

elements.text: There are two costly confirmation queries,
is-spent
and
is-spendable
, Last month I used a new
prevout
table to allow for precalculation of
is-spendable

in the validation phase, with completion on the confirmation phase. This reduced the amount of sequential computation in that query to the minimal strictly necessary. I hadn't been able to figure out a way to do this with the other query. On the big machine, during pure confirmation, there is now very little resource usage, due to query optimizations. So at least 50x more work could be done on this machine if
is-spent

could be parallelized except for the strictly necessary checks.

Last night I figured out how to move the entire
is-spent

query into the validation phase, except for a final check which in a typical run will always be a no-op. This won't necessarily help a lot on the mini without paging optimizations, and I have a couple more in mind. But it finally gets us to the point where the implementation maps to the theoretical ordering constraints.

As with the
is-spendable

optimization, this moves the costly part of the query to validation, where it can be parallel by block given all previous blocks are archived. The result of the precomputation is moved via the store to the confirmation phase in a block of fully-disposable data (can be purged during start, stop, and/or snapshot). In the
is-spendable

case the data required a 4 byte primary key for the parent tx of every spend. This is already read during validation, so it was free except for the temporary table.

In the
is-spent

case we need to identify the same primary key of the parent tx of any conflicting spends. This is a value also obtained during validation, as is the hash of every input point. So precomputation saves these redundant reads of the "self" spend identity. The costly part is the search in the
spent

table for conflicts (spends for every point, other than self). Turns out this query doesn't require total order, since it's not possible for a spending tx, introduced during validation (i.e. from the tx pool), to become confirmed in the interim. Only the instance of any tx, already associated with the block header at this point, will get marked as confirmed in the final confirmation step (due to enumeration of txs via the block association).

So the query can safely identify all spenders that might become confirmed in any previous block, and save the parent pk of those to the temporary table. This is typically going to be zero, and can be implemented with a prefix count value in order to differentiate from the
is-spendable

values in the table. The confirmation phase then just checks these txs for confirmed-ness, and if so the block is invalid for double spend. Though again, in a typical run there are no such conflicts, so
is-spent
essentially becomes a no-op in the strictly-ordered confirmation phase.

elements.text:
Actually the confirmation phase is now just a tiny percentage of what it was previously, as most of the work has been moved into the validation phase. That tiny percentage is small/fast enough that it gets subsumed by validation/download processing, so the CPU stays at 100% instead of everything waiting on slow confirmations.

An entire table has been removed from the process, since that data was already readily available during validation.

All of the costly confirmation querying has been moved to the parallel-by-block validation phase, which also means that there is no need for those queries to be in parallel std lib loops. This removes a lot of threading overhead, since we are already paying for concurrency by block.

The prevout cache (passed from validation to confirmation phases) is 2x larger because I added the sequence value. This can be optimized by only storing the sequence after bip68 activates, and only storing it when the relative locktime bit is set. But even at full size it's not bad, and can be deleted at any snapshot/start/stop.

I can't say that this will help the mini, since it will remain a question of disk paging, but I expect material improvement on the maxi. But there has been a significant paging reduction for sure. The remaining cost of the confirmation paging is really just reading point hashes to identify hashmap conflicts. That has also been reduced significantly by passing the "self" hash directly from the deserialized block into the confirmation query.  I'm pretty sure that by splitting out the hashes form the point table this will be reduced even further.
